accepted_interpretation.source_support: Assuming GRH for Dirichlet L-functions, the paper states that every odd integer greater than 5 is a sum of three primes. Its announced proof has three parts: a large-input asymptotic theorem, a lemma locating a prime near an unchecked odd integer, and computation of two-prime representations for the resulting differences.
accepted_interpretation.speculation_status: The conclusion is conditional on GRH. Neither the asymptotic statement nor the finite computation alone covers all inputs, and the source only outlines the three components here. Powers of ten are visibly OCR-degraded; the architecture and conditional theorem are clear, but exact historical thresholds require checking the scan. Describing the three parts as a compatible-threshold coverage argument and n-p as their bridge is a reasonable conceptual compression of the outline. The extracted powers of ten are visibly corrupted, so none of the exact historical thresholds should be reused without the scan.

accepted_interpretation.source_support: The unit defines a von-Mangoldt-weighted count J(N), introduces S(a), and expresses J(N) through an integral of S(a)^3 against the Nth Fourier mode, up to a stated error. parents.title: Use a GRH Chebyshev bound to leave a small even remainder

No material unsupported claim is present; the analysis does not assert unverified exact constants beyond the OCR-qualified value. Low: the finite-scale constant comparison and interface failure condition are specific, predictive consequences.
accepted_interpretation.source_support: Using Schoenfeld's GRH bound for the Chebyshev function, the proof argues that an interval ending at n cannot be prime-free beyond a controlled length. It concludes that for the stated finite range there is a prime p with 4 at most n-p at most about 1.615 times 10^12.
accepted_interpretation.speculation_status: A nominally sharper one-log estimate is reported to have a worse constant near the relevant scale. The short-interval contradiction and interface role are clear, but exact constants and endpoints require scan verification. Theta notation, inequality directions, exponents, and the 1.615 times 10^12 endpoint need scan verification.

parents.title: Reduce binary Goldbach verification to coverage by shifted prime sets

accepted_interpretation.interpretation: The search is compressed from separate primality questions into a union-of-translates problem. Its dominant cost is rebuilding the large prime set Q for each interval, which identifies the representation rather than the logical test as the computational bottleneck.
accepted_interpretation.nonparaphrase_operation: Shifted prime sets Q+p_i encode all witnesses supplied by one p_i at once; full interval coverage is the certificate of exhaustive verification.
accepted_interpretation.quality_reason: The verified two-prime range, the conventional construction of Q(a,b), the monotone unions Q(a,b)+p_i, exhaustive interval coverage, and the repeated sieve cost are explicit. No material unsupported claim is present; the analysis does not infer code-level guarantees or repair damaged set notation. Low: it identifies the representation and computational bottleneck rather than merely restating Goldbach verification.
accepted_interpretation.source_support: The unit states a verified two-prime range and describes the conventional interval algorithm. For even e in [a,b], it seeks a small odd prime p_i with e-p_i prime, forms a prime set Q(a,b), and enlarges cumulative covered sets by Q(a,b)+p_i until all even numbers in the interval are covered.
accepted_interpretation.speculation_status: Coverage certifies existence but not a canonical representation. The method remains expensive because the sieve for Q is repeated, and the source's set symbols are OCR-damaged. The prose supports the set-coverage interpretation, but exact notation and some interval parameters should be checked against the source image. Interpreting the unions as a set-coverage representation and coverage as an existence certificate is a direct and useful abstraction of the algorithm. Set symbols, indices, and the exact definition of the margin E_a are degraded, although the surrounding prose makes the algorithm clear.

parents.title: Combine bounded pseudoprime tests with vectorized bitset unions

accepted_interpretation.interpretation: The reported computation has three distinct dependencies: bounded strong-pseudoprime implications for treating tested candidates as prime, the logical equivalence between shifted primality bits and covered Goldbach targets, and the correctness of the implementation and run that performed all required shifts. Word-level OR operations accelerate the second mechanism but do not themselves establish that the complete run was executed correctly. Thus the span supplies reported exhaustive computational evidence for its finite range, not an independently inspectable certificate: its narrative includes no code, logs, replay result, or retained final coverage array.
accepted_interpretation.nonparaphrase_operation: Factors the evidence into primality-test validity, coverage-logic validity, and implementation/execution provenance, while separating the logical role of complete bit coverage from the performance role of vectorized OR operations.
accepted_interpretation.quality_reason: Accepted: the representation and reported finite computation are concrete enough for a supported conceptual analysis, and the revision closes the critic-identified epistemic gap by avoiding certificate language and distinguishing mathematical assumptions from unverified execution provenance.
accepted_interpretation.source_support: The span cites explicit bounded strong-pseudoprime criteria, describes ODD as a long array of 64-bit words with one primality bit per odd number below the cutoff, and says each new covered set is formed by OR-ing an accumulated array with a shifted ODD array. It reports a Cray C98 execution covering even numbers above 4 x 10^11 through 10^13, along with timings and an extreme case requiring 328 nearby primes. Those execution claims are reported by the authors in this span; the precise thresholds, endpoints, timings, and example integers are extraction-sensitive.
accepted_interpretation.speculation_status: No independent replay or audit is inferred. The finite coverage, runtime, and extreme-case statements are retained explicitly as author-reported execution evidence, while the cited primality implications are conditional on their stated bounds and correct testing; no adjacent analytic claim is imported.

parents.title: Precompute a small-prime bitset and shift it by primes near the interval base

accepted_interpretation.interpretation: The gain comes from reversing what is reused: precompute the prime set P once and translate it by consecutive primes q_i near the interval base, so many tests of whether e-q_i is prime become the monotone coverage process F_{i+1}=F_i union (P+q_{i+1}). This exchanges generation of every prime in each high interval for a larger reusable set of smaller primes plus only k nearby primes. The uniform-density calculation merely suggests a workable k; an interval is established only when the actual union covers every even target. Because existence of some decomposition suffices, the method gains reuse while giving up control over whether the returned prime summand is extremal.
accepted_interpretation.nonparaphrase_operation: Decomposes the algorithm into a reusable translated representation, a heuristic resource-sizing argument, an exhaustive stopping condition, and an explicit witness-optimality loss; this identifies which efficiency claim is structural and which conclusion still requires checked coverage.
accepted_interpretation.quality_reason: Accepted: the interpretation retains the concrete set-translation mathematics, removes the unsupported bitset representation from this unit, and makes the heuristic-versus-certified-coverage distinction explicit while preserving the stated tradeoff.
accepted_interpretation.source_support: The span explicitly defines P as the odd primes up to about b-a, constructs successive unions P+q_i until all even numbers in [a,b] are covered, labels uniform distribution contrary to fact as the premise of the density estimate, and reports that k=360 sufficed in the experiments. It also contrasts the one-time larger prime-set construction with regenerating all primes in each interval and states that the resulting summand is generally neither smallest nor largest. Extracted interval sizes and prime-count figures remain OCR-sensitive.
accepted_interpretation.speculation_status: The reuse and simultaneous-coverage reading is a source-supported inference. The source itself presents the uniform-density model only as a heuristic, so it is not treated as a proof of coverage or generalized beyond the reported run; no cross-source claim is added.
